title: Tranquillity sent down
hook: He sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers (48:4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, fath mubin: Hudaybiyyah, the treaty that felt like losing and turned out to be a door. Your line was an opening. Did a small closure show you one? Day five hundred eighty-one, the end of the week.

Back at Hudaybiyyah, picture the camp the night the treaty was signed. Fourteen hundred people who had walked for days to reach the Ka'bah, told to turn around. Some angry, some confused, a few close to refusing. The Prophet ﷺ told them to sacrifice their animals and shave their heads right there, and at first, the reports say, nobody moved. Anyone who has stood in a room full of disappointed people knows that silence. The surah describes what came down into that silence.

Verse four of Surah Al-Fath, in Pickthall's translation: "He it is Who sent down peace of reassurance into the hearts of the believers that they might add faith unto their faith." Peace of reassurance is Pickthall's way of rendering one Arabic word: sakinah. Its root, s-k-n, means to be still, to settle, to come to rest. The same root gives maskan, a dwelling, the place where you settle, and sakan, the night or a spouse, in whom one finds rest. So sakinah is the stillness you can live inside. Notice the verb. It is sent down, like rain. The verse doesn't say the believers calmed themselves. It says calm was given into hearts that were agitated. And notice what it does: it adds faith to faith, as if faith can grow, layer on layer. The word shows up at other hard moments in the Qur'an too. In Surah At-Tawbah, it comes down on the Prophet in the cave during the migration, when only Abu Bakr was with him and the trackers were at the entrance. And a hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when people gather in a house of Allah to recite and study the Qur'an together, sakinah descends on them and mercy covers them. Scholars of language note that Hebrew has a related word, shekhinah, which in Jewish tradition names the divine presence dwelling among people. A shared root between neighbors. This week we've knelt with every nation, prayed at forty, listened with the jinn, planted our feet, unlocked the heart, found an opening, and now, the stillness that comes down.
screen: `SAKINAH: STILLNESS YOU CAN LIVE IN.` · `SENT DOWN, LIKE RAIN.` · `IN THE CAVE, AND IN THE CIRCLE.` · `FAITH ADDED TO FAITH.`

segments.voice: The practice: breathe slowly until calm. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Breathe in for a count of four. Out for a count of six. Again. Don't try to manufacture calm; the verse says it is sent. Just make room for it, the way you'd open a window and wait for the air. If thoughts rush in, let them pass and go back to the count. If you pray, you can ask for sakinah. The bell holds the time.
Sakinah. Stillness sent down into agitated hearts, from the root for settling and dwelling, in 48:4. Today's word.
Your line: tranquillity comes down. Today, in the most tense moment you face, breathe in for four and out for six once before you answer. Day five hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims ask for sakinah in their own supplications and seek it in gatherings for Qur'an recitation and study, which a hadith in Sahih Muslim connects with its descent.

pairs: to settle, to come to rest

myth: in 48:4 the believers calm themselves down
the verse says Allah sent sakinah down into their hearts.
the verse says faith can be added to faith
sakinah comes down so that they add faith to their faith.
a hadith links sakinah with gathering to recite the Qur'an
Sahih Muslim says it descends on such gatherings.

fork.setup: you're in the camp at Hudaybiyyah, told to sacrifice and shave though you never reached Mecca. what does 48:4 say came to the believers?
fork.reveal: stillness was sent down, and with it, faith added to faith.

original.note: Arabic: tranquillity, settled stillness; root s-k-n.

trapdoor: what you thought: tranquillity is a mood you work up.
what it means: a stillness sent down into anxious hearts, at Hudaybiyyah and in the cave.
what a scholar hears: root s-k-n, to dwell and settle (maskan, a home); Hebrew shekhinah is a related word for the divine presence.
